title: After the kettle
hookLine: habits hook onto cues, so attach practice to something you already do

lines: IT CAN PULL A NEW ONE OUT TOO.
cards: The alarm goes off, and a hand reaches for the phone before anyone has decided anything. Feet find the kitchen. The kettle goes on, the way a foot finds the brake.
Nobody used willpower for any of that. The moment did the deciding. That sounds like bad news for anyone trying to build a new practice.
It's actually useful news. If a moment can pull the old habits out of you, it can pull a new one out too.

teach.h: FOUR IN TEN ACTIONS ON AUTOPILOT.
teach.b: First, how much of the day runs on autopilot. The psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues asked people to write down what they were doing and thinking through the day.
Roughly four in ten actions were done in the same place, almost every day, often while thinking about something else. Habits aren't laziness; they're how a busy brain saves effort.
Second, habits hook onto cues: a place, a time, an object, or the thing you just finished. The kettle clicks, and something follows.
So instead of adding a practice to your day as a brand new event, you hang it on a hook that's already there. Third, say it as a plan.
The psychologist Peter Gollwitzer studied what he called implementation intentions, plans in the form: if this happens, then I'll do that.
Across many studies, people who made a specific if-then plan followed through more often than people who only set a goal. I want to meditate more is a wish.
After I switch the kettle on, I sit for two minutes while it boils: that's a plan. Fourth, the traditions on this path tie practice to cues too. The Muslim prayers are set by the sun.
Jewish blessings come before bread and after. Catholic tradition rings a church bell for the Angelus in the morning, at noon and in the evening. Monks keep hours.
Nobody had to remember to be devout at random; the day itself tapped them on the shoulder.
The cue does the remembering, and you do the practice.

how: Some people tie a daily practice to an existing cue, such as sitting for two minutes after switching on the kettle; several traditions set prayer by the sun, the meal or a bell.

o: strong goals you hold firmly in mind each morning
rewards you give yourself after finishing a task
if-then plans that tie an action to a set moment

games.q: cues and plans — tap the pairs.
p: about four in ten actions are habits
a place, a time, or what just ended

s: habits are a sign of laziness
they're how a busy brain saves effort; roughly four in ten daily actions run that way.
a specific if-then plan tends to beat a general goal
Gollwitzer's implementation intentions: people followed through more often.
the best cue is a rare, special moment
an everyday cue works better, because it comes back every day.

games.q: you want to sit for two minutes every day. which plan is most likely to stick?
o: after I switch on the kettle, I sit while it boils.
every day, no matter what, somehow.
games.why: a specific cue with a specific action is an implementation intention, and studies find those get followed through more often.

practice: Walk through tomorrow morning in your mind, slowly, from waking up, and find the moments that happen every single day: feet on the floor, the kettle, unlocking the car.
Pick one, the more boring the better, and finish the sentence quietly: after this, I will do that, for two minutes. Then sit, and let the plan settle.

wordCard.voice: Implementation intentions, if-then plans like hanging a new practice on something you already do every day.

carryVoice: Your line: the cue does the remembering. Even thirty seconds after the cue still counts. Day three hundred eleven, done.
